blocks.text: The chapter describes tongues as prayer, praise, mystery, meaningful sound, speech that may be interpreted, self-edification, and speech outsiders do not understand. No audio sample survives, so Acts 2, a modern practice, or one ancient parallel cannot predetermine whether Corinthian tongues were human languages, ecstatic speech, or another Spirit-related phenomenon. In the gathered church, the practical rule is clearer than the phenomenon's classification: speech is limited, sequenced, and dependent on interpretation so that others can understand.

Prophecy is preferred in the assembly because it addresses people with upbuilding, encouragement, and consolation, while uninterpreted tongues do not instruct them. Paul joins spirit and mind rather than opposing them, and he treats prophecy as accountable speech: two or three may speak, others weigh what is said, speakers yield their turns, and prophetic spirits remain subject to prophets. Claimed revelation therefore does not end communal discernment.

The Isaiah quotation and the statement about tongues as a sign sit beside two sharply contrasting visitor scenes: undifferentiated tongues lead outsiders to call the gathering mad, while intelligible prophecy exposes what is hidden and redirects a visitor toward God. This tension resists turning the paragraph into a simple endorsement of public spectacle. Throughout the chapter, edification, intelligibility, learning, encouragement, self-control, peace, ordered participation, and evaluation explain what the regulations are for.

All extant Greek witnesses contain verses 34-35, though some Western witnesses place them after verse 40. Within the chapter, the same verb for keeping silent applies to an uninterpreted tongue speaker, a prophet who yields to another revelation, and women or wives in the disputed verses. The letter also assumes elsewhere that women pray and prophesy. These facts require textual honesty and make both effortless deletion and an unqualified permanent ban on women's speech difficult; the precise activity and scope being regulated remain disputed.

sections.title: Love and the Wider Gift Discussion

blocks.text: Chapter 13 stands between the gift discussions of chapters 12 and 14, where it corrects rivalry, noise, self-display, and knowledge used competitively rather than functioning primarily as romantic sentiment. Its description of love as patient, kind, truthful, and unwilling to insist on its own way supplies controls for correction, gifts, leadership, and reconciliation: spiritual activity cannot be separated from truth and noncoercion.

Acts describes Pentecost as recognizable languages or dialects heard by an international gathering. Its relation to other early Christian speech phenomena remains debated, so that multilingual scene can illuminate the larger subject without being forced into an exact definition of what occurred at Corinth.

Because the chapter's order serves intelligibility, shared participation, peace, and evaluation, it cannot be turned into a slogan for leader convenience, monopolized speech, gendered silencing, disability exclusion, or suppression of questions and abuse reports. Nor does this chapter supply medical criteria for diagnosing seizures, psychosis, trauma responses, neurodivergence, disability, or involuntary behavior as a spiritual failure; such judgments require qualified assessment, consent, and urgent care when needed.
